_note: Informal Portuguese, slang and swear words in Portugal (/conhecimentos/giria). Own draft, idioms-mistakes run (2026-11-20), not yet reviewed by a native speaker. reg: umgang (informal) | slang | vulgaer (rude); stufe (vulgaer only): 1 mild, 2 strong, 3 very strong. w, bsp and the hoeflich pairs are Portuguese; std is the standard word with its English meaning; info is English. variety on every entry, a ptBR note where Brazil differs. No slurs and no insults about groups of people (content-plan §5.7).

stufen.name: Standard Portuguese
stufen.satz: Pode esperar um momento, por favor?

stufen.name: Rude
stufen.satz: Espera aí, porra, que já vou!

gruppen.titel: Short forms: how people really speak
gruppen.intro: In everyday speech, Portuguese swallows sounds, especially in Portugal. Don't write these forms in a letter or an exam, but you will hear them every day and see them in messages.

eintraege.std: estou, estás, está (I am, you are, he/she is)
eintraege.bsp: Tou a chegar, já tás aí?
eintraege.info: Very common in speech and chats. In writing, use the full forms.
Many people say pra even when they write para. In an exam or a formal letter, write para.

eintraege.bsp: A gente vai ao café logo à noite?
eintraege.info: Colloquial "we". The verb stays in the 3rd person singular: a gente vai, not a gente vamos. Common in speech, avoid it in formal writing.
Short for vamos embora. Used among friends and colleagues.

eintraege.bsp: A stora de Matemática é fixe.
eintraege.info: School and university slang, used by students; to address your teacher use Professor or Professora.

ptBR.note: Not used in Brazil. The usual word is o professor, o prof.

eintraege.w: o frigo, a tele, a net
eintraege.std: o frigorífico, a televisão, a internet (fridge, TV, internet)
eintraege.bsp: Está no frigo. Vamos ver a tele?
eintraege.info: Everyday short forms.

ptBR.note: In Brazil: a geladeira (not frigo), a TV.

eintraege.info: Friendly and warm. A man says obrigadinho, a woman obrigadinha: the ending follows the speaker.

gruppen.intro: These words are relaxed, but not rude. With friends and colleagues they are normal. In a formal letter or at an office, use the word on the right.

eintraege.info: Between friends it is warm. With strangers or at the office it can sound rude. Typical of Portugal.

ptBR.note: Not used this way in Brazil.

eintraege.info: One of the most typical Portugal words. It is safe in any informal situation.

eintraege.bsp: Que casa gira! Ele é muito giro.
eintraege.info: About a person it can mean good-looking. Very common in Portugal.

ptBR.note: In Brazil: bonito, legal; giro is not used.

eintraege.std: o homem, a mulher, o tipo (guy, woman)
eintraege.info: Colloquial for "the guy". Use it only among friends: in some contexts, especially about a woman, it sounds disrespectful.
Short agreement, "yes, I know". Pois não means "of course, yes please"; pois, pois can be ironic ("sure, sure"). Typical of Portugal.
Very common. It has nothing to do with calhar as a verb: learn it as one phrase.

ptBR.note: In Brazil: talvez is the usual word.

eintraege.std: resolver sozinho (to get by, to manage)
eintraege.bsp: Não falo bem português, mas desenrasco-me.
eintraege.info: A very typical Portuguese word: to solve a problem with what you have. O desenrascanço is that clever improvisation.
A small, cheap place with home cooking. Said with affection: it is a compliment.

eintraege.bsp: Que dia chato! Que reunião chata!
eintraege.info: About a person it can sound rude.

eintraege.bsp: Cuidado com aquele aldrabão: prometeu e não fez nada.
eintraege.info: Aldrabar = to cheat, to lie. Strong for a person: don't say it to someone's face.

eintraege.bsp: Espera um bocadinho. Estou um bocado cansada.
eintraege.info: Bocadinho is the smaller, friendlier version. Both are very common.

ptBR.note: In Brazil: um pouco, um pouquinho.

eintraege.info: In Lisbon uma bica is an espresso; in the north people say um café or um cimbalino. Um café gets you an espresso everywhere.

ptBR.note: Not used in Brazil. A café is a coffee, usually served from a pot.

eintraege.info: Used for exams and tests; not for people. The opposite is passar or ser aprovado. Estar chumbado = to have failed.

eintraege.bsp: Estou de rastos depois do treino.
eintraege.info: Used for being very tired or defeated; friendly and common.

gruppen.intro: In class you learn the normal words. You will still hear these a lot: you need to understand them, but you don't have to say them.

eintraege.bsp: Não tenho massa para as férias.
eintraege.info: Not only the pasta! Very common among friends.

eintraege.bsp: Esta casa custa uma pipa de massa.
eintraege.info: A pipa is a big barrel. Used about expensive things.
A tostão was an old coin. It means "very cheap".
About a short period. Don't say it to your landlord on rent day.

eintraege.std: e um pouco mais (and a bit more)
eintraege.bsp: São duas e picos. Tem trinta e tal anos.
eintraege.info: After a number it means "a little more than". E tal and e picos are both common in Portugal.
Also: uma carrada de. Both are informal.
About a bill that is far too high. Literally: a stab.

gruppen.intro: Slang changes fast. Young people use it with each other. An adult who uses it at the office often sounds strange.

eintraege.info: From Angolan Portuguese. Common among young people in Portugal; in writing and at work, use muito.
A filler, like English "like". Very common among young people; too much sounds careless.
Written ya or yá; typical of young people in Portugal. Not Brazilian.
Also: curtir uma noite = to enjoy a night out. Informal.
Between friends, also with siblings. Used a lot by young people in cities.

eintraege.std: a pessoa mais velha (an older person)
eintraege.bsp: O cota do meu pai deu-me boleia.
eintraege.info: Friendly slang for an older person, often a parent or an experienced colleague.
Bazar is a verb here, not the shop. Informal.

eintraege.std: a coisa, a situação (the thing, the deal)
eintraege.bsp: Gostei da cena da festa. Qual é a cena?
eintraege.info: A cena fills many gaps: "the thing". Informal.
From English, used by young people. The Portuguese word is constrangedor or embaraçoso.

eintraege.std: ficar sem dinheiro ou energia (to run out)
eintraege.bsp: Fiquei a zero depois do jantar.
eintraege.info: Of money or battery. Informal.

gruppen.intro: You'll hear swear words in Portugal more often than in many countries, in the street, on TV and at work. You should understand them, but saying them yourself is risky: as a foreigner you can quickly sound aggressive.

eintraege.info: Mild and friendly. Fine in almost any company.
A softened swear word. It is fine even with colleagues.
Says surprise, shock or disgust. Mild.
Used among friends. About a stranger it is an insult.
A direct insult. Don't use it about people who are present.
Rude when it is aimed at someone. Between close friends it can be a joke.

eintraege.bsp: Estou-me nas tintas para o que ele pensa.
eintraege.info: Colloquial and strong. It says that someone doesn't care at all.
The standard swear word of annoyance. Strong in a formal setting; common among friends.
Very common in Portugal, stronger than bolas. At work it is often tolerated; in front of strangers it sounds rough.
A strong way to tell someone to go away. Never at the office.

eintraege.std: pessoa desagradável (bastard, but can be friendly)
eintraege.bsp: Aquele cabrão não pagou a renda.
eintraege.info: Between male friends, it can be affectionate. About someone who isn't a friend, it is a strong insult.
Very common and very strong. Learn to understand it, not to say it.
A very strong word, very common in Portugal as an intensifier. Never in an office or with strangers.

hoeflich.zu: Podes falar mais baixo, por favor?
Podes esperar um momento, por favor?
